metadata.note: Security guards 1.28M (BLS May 2025). Covers the limits of authority and why observe, record and call is the default, patrol discipline and never falsifying checkpoints, incident report writing that survives court, access control and tailgating, CCTV privacy and evidence handling, alarm and fire response, lone working, and the supervisor and site risk assessment track.

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and your security experience.

key_points: Setting first, because the job is completely different in each: corporate reception, retail, hospital, school, construction site, event, warehouse, residential, night patrol
Licence and clearances: security licence or registration where required, first aid, background check, and whether they are current
Scale: site size, number of access points, cameras monitored, patrol route length, shift pattern, whether you worked alone
What you actually did: access control, patrol, CCTV monitoring, incident response, reporting, alarm response, visitor management, conflict de-escalation
One outcome: an incident handled well, a pattern you spotted, a procedure you improved, an accident free record
Say whether you have worked unsupervised overnight, since most of this work is exactly that
strong_answer_signals: Names the setting, which decides whether experience transfers
Licence status stated without being asked
Comfortable working alone overnight
avoid: Being vague about licence or clearance status
Describing the job as watching a screen
No mention of reporting or documentation

questions.text: Tell me about an incident you handled.

key_points: Situation: what happened. A theft, a trespass, a medical emergency, a fire alarm, an aggressive person, a dispute, an unauthorised access attempt
Action: assess the risk first, then respond within your authority and the site instructions
Say who you called and when. Calling early is the correct answer in almost every case
Observe and record: description, time, location, what was said, what you did
Result: the outcome and the report you filed
Say what changed afterwards, such as a procedure, a lock, a light, or a patrol timing
strong_answer_signals: Assesses risk before acting
Calls for support early
Files a complete report
avoid: Physical intervention as the first response
Handling a serious incident alone to prove capability
A story with no report at the end

questions.text: Tell me about a time you de-escalated a confrontation.

key_points: Situation: an angry customer, an intoxicated person, a refused entry, a trespass, a dispute between two people
Action: calm voice, open posture, keep your distance, and give them space and time. Never crowd someone who is agitated
Explain rather than command where you can. Most escalation comes from tone, not content
Offer a face saving way out. People escalate when they feel cornered or humiliated
Know when to stop talking and call for support. Talking longer is not always the safer option
Result: it ended without force, and what you recorded
strong_answer_signals: Names distance and posture, not just tone
Gives a face saving exit
Knows when talking stops working
avoid: Escalating by asserting authority
Cornering someone physically
A story where force was the resolution

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked a long or quiet shift.

key_points: Be honest: much of this work is long and uneventful, and staying alert through it is the actual skill
Action: how you stay effective. Varying patrol timings and routes, active observation rather than passive watching, staying off your phone, using the shift for checks that need doing
Say how you manage fatigue on nights: sleep routine, breaks, movement
Result: the site secure and the checks completed and logged
Say what you did during a quiet shift that turned out to matter
strong_answer_signals: Varies patrol timing and route deliberately
Active observation rather than passive watching
Honest about managing fatigue
avoid: Phone use on shift
Predictable patrol timing
Treating a quiet shift as time off

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to refuse someone entry.

key_points: Situation: no identification, not on the list, an expired pass, intoxication, a banned individual, or wrong site
Action: be polite, firm and consistent. Explain the rule rather than hiding behind it, and offer the route if one exists
Do not negotiate on a rule you do not have authority to waive. Check with the right person instead of guessing
Watch for tailgating behind you while you are dealing with the person in front
Result: entry refused, the person handled without escalation, and the incident logged
Say that consistency is what protects you here. Making exceptions creates the next argument
strong_answer_signals: Consistent regardless of who is asking
Watches for tailgating during a distraction
Logs the refusal
avoid: Letting someone in because they were senior or persistent
Refusing rudely and creating a confrontation
Not recording the refusal

questions.text: Tell me about a mistake you made on duty.

key_points: Real examples: missing a check, a gap in the log, letting someone tailgate, a delayed report, an alarm handled incorrectly, missing something on camera
Own it and report it immediately. In security a hidden gap is what an investigation finds later
Action: what you did to correct it and who you told
Result and the specific habit that changed
Say why an accurate record matters more than a clean one
strong_answer_signals: Reports rather than covering the gap
Names the habit change
Understands an accurate log beats a clean log
avoid: Saying you have never made one
Filling in a log afterwards to look complete
Blaming the equipment or the shift before

questions.text: Tell me about a time you spotted something before it became a problem.

key_points: Options: a propped door, a broken lock or light, an unfamiliar vehicle returning, a person watching a building, a fire exit blocked, a pattern on camera
Action: what you noticed and why it stood out. Say the baseline, because noticing means knowing what normal looks like
Report it and record it, and follow up on whether it was fixed
Result: the incident prevented, or the vulnerability closed
Say that most prevention is boring and repetitive, which is why it works
strong_answer_signals: Knows the baseline for the site, which is what makes anomalies visible
Follows up on whether it was fixed
Values prevention over response
avoid: Only describing responses to incidents, never prevention
Reporting once and never checking
Waiting for something to happen

questions.text: Tell me about working with police or emergency services.

key_points: Say what your role is: secure the scene, preserve evidence, control access, brief the responders, and stay out of the way of their job
Action: give a clear factual brief. What happened, when, where, who is involved, what you have done, and what access they need
Have the information ready: camera footage times, keys, floor plans, contact numbers
Do not investigate. Your job ends where theirs begins
Result: the handover and the report
Say how you recorded the details before memory faded
strong_answer_signals: Briefs clearly and factually
Preserves the scene and evidence
Does not investigate
avoid: Trying to solve the crime yourself
Contaminating a scene
A vague handover with no times or detail

questions.text: Tell me about feedback you received.

key_points: Real feedback here: incomplete reports, predictable patrol timing, tone with the public, phone use, missed checks, sloppy access control
Action: how you asked what the standard was and what you changed
Result: the audit passed, the complaint stopped, the log complete
Say whether the feedback came from a client or a supervisor, since client perception is a large part of this job
strong_answer_signals: Takes it without defending
Change is observable in the records
Understands client perception matters
avoid: Feedback that was really praise
Disagreeing with the standard
No evidence of change

questions.text: Tell me about a time you dealt with a member of the public who needed help.

key_points: Security is customer facing far more often than it is confrontational. Say that, because many candidates miss it
Situations: directions, a lost person, a medical issue, a distressed person, a lost child, someone locked out
Action: be approachable and helpful, and know the site well enough to actually help
For a medical or a vulnerable person: follow the procedure, call for the right help, and stay with them
Result: the person helped and the incident recorded where required
Say that being visible and approachable is itself a deterrent
strong_answer_signals: Recognises the customer service half of the job
Knows the site well enough to help
Visible presence framed as deterrence
avoid: Treating the public as a nuisance
Only describing enforcement
Leaving a distressed person to find someone else

questions.text: What are the limits of your authority?

key_points: Be clear and confident about this, because it is the most important technical question in the interview
You are not a police officer. You observe, report, deter, and control access on private property
Detention powers are limited and vary by jurisdiction. Know what your licence and your site instructions actually permit, and never exceed them
Use of force, where permitted at all, is a last resort, must be reasonable and proportionate, and is only for defence or prevention of harm
You cannot search a person without consent in most contexts, and you cannot detain on suspicion alone
When in doubt, observe, record and call the police. That is almost always the correct answer
Say that exceeding your authority exposes you personally to criminal and civil liability
strong_answer_signals: Clear that they are not police
Knows detention and search limits vary and are narrow
Defaults to observe, record, call
avoid: Claiming powers you do not have
Describing a search or detention casually
Any answer where force is an early option

questions.text: How do you conduct a patrol?

key_points: Vary the timing and the route. A predictable patrol is a timetable for anyone watching
Use all your senses, not just sight. Sound and smell find things cameras never will, such as a gas leak, a fire, or someone in a stairwell
Know what normal looks like for the site, so an anomaly stands out
Check the specifics: doors and windows secure, fire exits clear and unlocked from inside, lighting working, alarms set, plant rooms, roof access, perimeter, vehicles
Use the patrol system or checkpoints honestly. Logging a checkpoint you did not visit is a serious integrity failure
Record what you found, including nothing to report, since the record is the proof of service
strong_answer_signals: Varies timing and route
Knows the site baseline
Never logs a checkpoint they did not visit
avoid: The same route at the same time every night
Logging checkpoints from the office
Only checking what the system prompts

questions.text: How do you write an incident report?

key_points: Facts only, in chronological order, in plain language. No opinion, no speculation about motive, no conclusions
Cover the basics: who, what, when, where, how you became aware, what you did, who you notified, what the outcome was
Be specific: exact times, exact locations, descriptions with detail, and direct quotes where you can remember them
Write it as soon as possible while memory is accurate, and never alter a report afterwards. Add a supplementary note instead
Assume it will be read in court or by a regulator, because it might be
Attach the evidence: camera times, photographs where appropriate, names of witnesses
strong_answer_signals: Facts only, no speculation
Written immediately, never altered afterwards
Assumes it will be read in court
avoid: Writing what you think happened
Vague times and descriptions
Amending an earlier report rather than adding a supplement

questions.text: How do you handle access control and visitor management?

key_points: Verify before granting: identification, the expected list, the host, and the purpose
Issue and record passes properly, and make sure they are returned. Unreturned passes are a live vulnerability
Escort where the policy requires it, and never let a visitor into a restricted area unescorted
Watch for tailgating, which is the most common way sites are breached. Challenge it politely every time
Deliveries and contractors: verify the company, the job, and the authorisation. Social engineering usually arrives in a uniform
Never share codes, never lend a pass, and never prop a door
Say that consistency is the control. An exception once becomes the expectation
strong_answer_signals: Names tailgating as the main breach route
Sceptical of uniforms and urgency
Consistency framed as the control
avoid: Letting someone in because they looked official
Propping a door for a contractor
Not tracking pass returns

questions.text: What do you know about CCTV monitoring?

key_points: Know the purpose and the legal frame: cameras must be used for the stated purpose, and there are privacy rules about where they can point and who can view footage
Active monitoring is different from watching. Scan systematically, follow up anything unusual, and know your camera coverage and blind spots
Log what you observe with camera number and time, so footage can be retrieved later
Retrieval and evidence handling: know the procedure, maintain the chain of custody, and never share footage informally
Never use cameras to watch individuals for personal reasons, and never point them at areas where people expect privacy
Report faults immediately. A camera that has been down for a week is a gap nobody knows about
strong_answer_signals: Knows privacy rules and stated purpose
Logs camera number and time for later retrieval
Reports faults rather than working around them
avoid: Sharing footage informally
Using cameras to watch a specific person without cause
Not knowing the blind spots on your own site

questions.text: How do you respond to an alarm activation?

key_points: Treat every activation as genuine until proven otherwise. Complacency about false alarms is how real ones get missed
Follow the response procedure: identify the zone, approach with caution, observe before entering, and call for support before you commit
Do not enter alone where the procedure says otherwise, and never confront a suspected intruder alone
Check the cause: a genuine intrusion, a fault, an environmental trigger, or a staff error
Reset and record properly, including the cause where you can establish it
Report repeat false alarms so the fault is fixed, since repeated false alarms erode the response
strong_answer_signals: Treats every alarm as genuine
Observes before entering and calls support
Reports repeat false alarms as a fault to fix
avoid: Assuming it is another false alarm
Entering a zone alone against procedure
Resetting without recording the cause

questions.text: What do you know about fire safety and emergency evacuation?

key_points: Know your role in the plan: raise the alarm, call the fire service, direct people, sweep assigned areas if that is your role, and go to the assembly point
Life safety before property, always. Nothing on the site is worth staying for
Know the escape routes, the assembly points, the fire panel, and where the extinguishers and hoses are
Only tackle a fire if it is small, you are trained, you have a clear escape route, and it is your role to do so
Keep fire exits and routes clear on every patrol. A blocked exit is one of the most common and most dangerous findings
Account for people at the assembly point and brief the fire service on arrival
Know the arrangements for anyone needing assistance to evacuate
strong_answer_signals: Life safety before property
Knows the personal evacuation arrangements for people needing help
Checks exits on every patrol
avoid: Going back into a building for property
Tackling a fire beyond training or without an escape route
Not knowing the assembly point

questions.text: How do you handle a medical emergency?

key_points: Call emergency services first or delegate the call clearly to a named person. Never assume someone else has called
Scene safety before anything else. You cannot help if you become a second casualty
Give first aid within your training only, and say what your training level is honestly
Send someone to meet and direct the ambulance, and clear access for them
Keep the person calm and stay with them, and keep others back for their dignity
Record it: time of collapse, time of call, what was done, who attended
Follow up on the automated defibrillator location and readiness, since knowing where it is beforehand is the whole point
strong_answer_signals: Delegates the call to a named person
Scene safety first
Knows the defibrillator location in advance
avoid: Acting beyond your first aid training
Assuming someone else called
Leaving the casualty to manage the scene

questions.text: How do you handle theft or suspected theft?

key_points: Observe and report. Do not chase, do not confront, and do not touch, unless site policy and your training specifically permit it and it is safe
In retail, the legal test for any approach is usually strict and continuous observation. If you did not see the whole sequence, you do not have it
Record what you can: description, clothing, direction, time, camera number, vehicle and plate
Alert the right people discreetly: the manager, the control room, or the police
Preserve evidence and secure the footage before it is overwritten
Never accuse anyone, and never act on appearance rather than behaviour
Say that your safety and the company liability both point the same way here
strong_answer_signals: Refuses to chase or confront
Knows continuous observation is required before any approach
Secures footage before it is overwritten
avoid: Chasing someone off site
Accusing a customer
Profiling based on appearance

questions.text: What do you know about health and safety on a site?

key_points: Security staff usually see more of the site than anyone else, so you are the most likely person to spot a hazard
Common findings: blocked fire exits, trailing cables, spills, faulty lighting, damaged flooring, unsecured ladders, propped doors, expired extinguishers
Report and where possible make safe immediately with signage or a barrier
Know the site specific risks: traffic and vehicle movements, plant, chemicals, height, confined spaces
Follow the permit to work system where the site has one, and know who is allowed where
Wear the required protective equipment on industrial and construction sites, and enforce it consistently
Record hazards and follow up. A hazard reported three times and never fixed needs escalating
strong_answer_signals: Sees themselves as the eyes of the site
Makes safe immediately, then reports
Escalates a hazard that keeps being ignored
avoid: Walking past a hazard because it is not your department
Not wearing required protective equipment yourself
Reporting once and dropping it

questions.text: How do you handle confidentiality and data?

key_points: Everything you see on a site is confidential: people, documents, footage, access records, incidents
Do not discuss incidents outside the professional circle, including with family or on social media. Posting about a site is a dismissal offence in most companies
Camera footage and access logs are personal data with legal protection. Handle, share and retain them only through the proper process
Never take photographs of a site or an incident on a personal device unless the procedure requires it
Verify identity before releasing any information, including to someone claiming to be from the client
Say that discretion is most of what a client is paying for
strong_answer_signals: Knows footage and access logs are protected personal data
No social media, no personal device photographs
Verifies identity before releasing information
avoid: Discussing an incident outside work
Posting anything about the site online
Sharing footage informally with a manager who asked

questions.text: How do you hand over to the next shift?

key_points: A proper handover is the difference between a site with continuity and one with a gap every twelve hours
Cover what the next person actually needs: incidents, ongoing situations, faults, people to watch for, contractors on site, keys and equipment, alarm status
Do it in writing as well as verbally, since verbal handovers are forgotten and disputed
Check the equipment together: radios, keys, torches, and the log
Do not leave until the relief has arrived and been briefed, unless the procedure allows otherwise
Read the previous handover at the start of your own shift rather than assuming nothing happened
strong_answer_signals: Written as well as verbal
Checks equipment and keys together
Reads the previous handover before starting
avoid: A verbal handover only
Leaving before the relief is briefed
Starting a shift without reading what happened

questions.text: You find someone in the building who should not be there. What do you do?

key_points: Assess before approaching: how many people, are they agitated, do they appear armed, where are your exits, do you have a radio
Do not approach alone if there is any doubt. Call for support or the police first and observe from a safe position
If you do approach: identify yourself, keep your distance, stay between them and your exit, and use a calm non confrontational opening
Most cases are innocent: a contractor, a lost visitor, an employee working late. Start there rather than with an accusation
If they are not authorised, ask them to leave and escort them off if it is safe. Do not detain
Record everything and check the footage
Report how they got in, since that is the real issue
strong_answer_signals: Assesses before approaching
Starts from an innocent explanation
Reports the access failure, not just the person
avoid: Approaching an unknown person alone in an isolated area
Detaining someone without authority
Only reporting the person and not how they got in

questions.text: An employee asks you to let them into a restricted area without a pass.

key_points: Politely decline and follow the procedure. Being known to them does not authorise access
Verify through the proper route: a supervisor, the control room, or the access list
Explain the rule plainly. Most people accept a rule applied to everyone
Log the request and the outcome
Report a pattern. Someone repeatedly asking for an exception is either a process problem or a red flag
Say that the moment you make one exception, every future refusal becomes an argument
strong_answer_signals: Verifies through the proper route
Logs the request
Recognises a repeated pattern as a signal
avoid: Letting a familiar face through
Making an exception for a senior person
Not logging the request

questions.text: Someone becomes aggressive towards you. What do you do?

key_points: Your safety comes first. No site, no property, and no rule is worth an injury
Create distance and keep a clear exit behind you. Never let yourself be backed into a corner
Stay calm, keep your hands visible and open, and lower your voice rather than raising it
Call for support early rather than when it has already escalated
Disengage if it continues. Walking away and calling the police is a professional response, not a failure
Never use force except as a last resort to protect yourself or someone else, and only within your training and the law
Record it fully afterwards and report it, including near misses
strong_answer_signals: Safety and exit route as the first consideration
Calls support early
Disengagement framed as professional
avoid: Standing your ground to avoid backing down
Using force to assert authority
Not reporting because nothing actually happened

questions.text: You suspect an employee of theft. What do you do?

key_points: Do not confront, accuse, or investigate. Internal theft is a management and sometimes a police matter
Record what you actually observed, factually, with times and camera references
Report through the proper channel, which may be a manager, a loss prevention team, or a confidential line
Preserve the evidence and secure the footage before it is overwritten
Keep it confidential. Discussing a suspicion with colleagues can destroy a case and damage an innocent person
Say plainly that suspicion is not proof and that your job is accurate observation
strong_answer_signals: Does not investigate or confront
Secures footage immediately
Keeps the suspicion confidential
avoid: Confronting the employee
Discussing it with other staff
Waiting to be sure before reporting

questions.text: A client asks you to do something outside your remit or against procedure.

key_points: Understand what they actually need, since there is often a legitimate way to achieve it
Explain what you can do and what you cannot, and why. Reference the assignment instructions rather than making it personal
Decline anything unsafe, unlawful, or outside your licence, calmly and without argument
Escalate to your supervisor or account manager rather than deciding alone. That is exactly what they are there for
Record the request and the outcome
Say that doing it to keep the client happy exposes you personally, and that your company would rather have the call
strong_answer_signals: Escalates rather than deciding alone
Records the request
Understands personal liability
avoid: Doing it because the client pays the contract
Refusing rudely without escalating
Not recording the request

questions.text: You are alone on site and something serious happens.

key_points: Call for external help first: police, fire, or ambulance as appropriate. Do not try to manage a serious incident alone
Then notify your control room or supervisor
Secure yourself first. You cannot help anyone if you are hurt
Do what you safely can: control access, direct people, preserve the scene, meet the emergency services
Record continuously as you go, since detail is lost quickly under stress
Say that your lone working procedure should include check in times and a plan if you do not check in, and ask whether the site has one
strong_answer_signals: Calls external help before internal
Secures self before acting
Asks about lone working check in arrangements
avoid: Trying to handle a serious incident alone
Notifying the supervisor before emergency services
No record because it was too busy

questions.text: You notice a colleague not following procedure.

key_points: Say something directly and privately first. Most of it is habit or shortcut rather than intent
Be specific: skipped patrol checks, logging checkpoints from the desk, propping doors, phone use, sleeping on shift, letting people in without checks
Escalate if it continues or if it is serious. Falsified logs and sleeping on duty are integrity issues, not minor ones
Understand the stakes: a colleague cutting corners creates a gap the whole site relies on being covered
Say plainly that covering for it makes you part of it, and that in a licensed industry it can affect your own registration
strong_answer_signals: Addresses it directly first
Treats falsified logs as an integrity issue
Understands their own licence is at risk
avoid: Saying nothing to avoid conflict
Covering a falsified log
Reporting it to everyone except a supervisor

questions.text: There is a bomb threat or a suspicious package.

key_points: Do not touch, move, or open anything. Do not use a radio or a mobile phone near a suspicious item where the procedure says otherwise
For a threat call: stay calm, keep the caller talking, note exact wording, listen for background sounds, and complete the threat checklist if the site has one
Notify the police and the site management immediately
Follow the decision on evacuation. Note that evacuating towards an unknown item can be more dangerous than staying, which is why the plan and the police decide, not you
Cordon and control access, and keep people away
Record everything precisely, including exact times and exact words
strong_answer_signals: Never touches or moves the item
Knows evacuation is a plan and police decision
Records exact wording of a threat call
avoid: Moving or examining a package
Deciding to evacuate independently
Paraphrasing a threat call from memory

questions.text: A camera or an access system is not working.

key_points: Report it immediately. A known gap can be covered, an unknown gap cannot
Compensate in the meantime: additional patrols of the affected area, a physical presence at the affected door, or manual logging
Record the fault, the time it started, and the mitigation you put in place. That record matters if something happens during the outage
Chase the repair rather than assuming it is in hand, and escalate if it drags
Check the whole system rather than assuming one fault is isolated
Say that an outage nobody compensated for is how sites get breached
strong_answer_signals: Compensates with presence or patrols
Records the outage and the mitigation
Chases the repair rather than assuming
avoid: Waiting for someone else to notice
Not adjusting patrols during the outage
No record of the outage period

questions.text: You are offered something by a contractor or a member of the public.

key_points: Decline politely. Gifts, favours and cash create an obligation and that is exactly the point of them
Report it, including small offers. A pattern of small favours is how access gets compromised
Follow the company gifts and hospitality policy, and record it where required
Be alert to grooming: repeated friendliness from someone who wants a door left open, a delivery unchecked, or a camera angle noted
Say plainly that your integrity is the product the client is buying
Never accept anything from someone whose access you control
strong_answer_signals: Declines and reports even small offers
Recognises grooming patterns
Understands integrity is the product
avoid: Accepting a small gift as harmless
Not reporting because you declined anyway
Building a friendship with someone whose access you control

questions.text: How do you supervise a security team?

key_points: Set clear assignment instructions and make sure every officer has read and understood them, including relief and temporary staff
Brief at shift change and check the handover actually happened
Visit the site on all shifts, including nights. A supervisor who has never seen the night shift does not know the site
Audit the records: patrol logs, incident reports, access logs. Look for the patterns that suggest checks are not being done
Coach on the things that matter: report quality, de-escalation, consistency at access control
Deal with integrity issues immediately and consistently. In this industry there is no small integrity issue
strong_answer_signals: Sees every shift including nights
Audits records for patterns
Zero tolerance on integrity, applied consistently
avoid: Supervising from reports alone
Never visiting the night shift
Inconsistent handling of falsified logs

questions.text: How do you carry out a site risk assessment?

key_points: Start from what you are protecting: people first, then assets, then information, then reputation and continuity
Identify the threats specific to this site: theft, violence, trespass, protest, vandalism, insider risk, and local crime patterns
Walk the site at different times, including at night and at shift change, since the vulnerabilities differ
Assess the layers: perimeter, building envelope, access control, internal zoning, detection, response, and procedure
Rate by likelihood and impact, and be honest about where the real gaps are rather than where the easy fixes are
Recommend proportionate measures with cost, and say what you would do first with no budget at all
Review it after any incident and on a schedule
strong_answer_signals: People before assets, stated explicitly
Walks the site at different times
Says what to do first with no budget
avoid: A generic assessment not specific to the site
Assessing only during the day
Recommendations with no prioritisation

questions.text: How do you handle an officer who falsified a patrol log?

key_points: Treat it as a serious integrity matter from the start. This is not a performance issue
Establish the facts properly: the system data, the camera footage, and the officer account, before concluding
Follow the disciplinary process exactly and fairly. A rushed process fails and the officer stays
Understand the consequence: a client relying on patrols that did not happen has been sold something they did not get, and it may be a contractual and licensing issue
Report to the client where the contract requires it, and be honest about it. Concealing it is worse than the original failure
Look at the system too: was the route achievable in the time, and was there pressure that made falsifying attractive
strong_answer_signals: Treats it as integrity, not performance
Honest with the client rather than concealing
Checks whether the route was achievable
avoid: Handling it informally to avoid losing a person
Concealing it from the client
Concluding before checking the data

questions.text: How do you manage client relationships on a security contract?

key_points: Understand what the client actually values, which is often visible presence and responsiveness rather than the number of patrols
Report proactively: incidents, trends, near misses, hazards found, and recommendations. A monthly report nobody reads is not communication
Be honest when something went wrong, quickly. Clients forgive incidents and do not forgive being told late
Turn incident data into advice: patterns, vulnerabilities, and what to fix
Manage scope honestly. Absorbing extra duties silently degrades the core service and then both fail
Review the assignment instructions with the client regularly, since sites change and instructions do not
strong_answer_signals: Reports trends, not just incidents
Honest and fast when something goes wrong
Manages scope creep explicitly
avoid: Only contacting the client at renewal
Hiding a service failure
Absorbing extra duties without a conversation

questions.text: How do you handle recruitment and turnover in security?

key_points: Screen properly: licence verification, background checks, employment history with gaps explained, and references actually taken
Never put someone on site before checks are complete, whatever the staffing pressure. This is the single biggest risk in the industry
Onboard to the site, not just to the company. Assignment instructions, a walk through, and a shadow shift
Understand why people leave: lone working with no support, unpredictable shifts, no equipment, no progression, and being treated as disposable
Give a path: supervisor, control room, CCTV, mobile patrol, corporate sites
Give the number: turnover, or average tenure, or vacancy fill time
strong_answer_signals: Never deploys before checks are complete
Onboards to the site, not just the company
Names lone working support as a retention issue
avoid: Putting someone on site pending checks
Induction that is paperwork only
Treating turnover as unavoidable

questions.text: How do you handle a serious incident as a manager?

key_points: People first: casualties, emergency services, and the safety of your officers and the public
Take control of the scene and the information. One person communicating prevents chaos and contradiction
Preserve evidence: footage secured before it is overwritten, statements taken while memory is fresh, the scene protected
Notify the client, your company, and the insurer per procedure, and be factual rather than defensive
Support the officers involved. Violence and serious incidents affect people for a long time and this is where a company is judged
Debrief and investigate for the system cause: procedure, staffing, equipment, training, or lighting
Follow through on the changes and tell the client what changed
strong_answer_signals: Secures footage before it is overwritten
Supports the officers involved
Investigates the system cause
avoid: Managing the message before the people
Sending a shaken officer straight back out
An investigation that ends at individual blame

questions.text: How do you manage scheduling and lone working?

key_points: Schedule to the risk profile of the site and the hours, not evenly. Nights and shift changes need more, not less
Manage fatigue deliberately: limit consecutive nights, watch excessive overtime, and build in rest between shifts
Lone working procedure with check in and check out, a defined escalation if a check is missed, and equipment that actually works
Publish rotas in advance. Unpredictable shifts are the biggest cause of turnover in this industry
Have a real cover plan rather than relying on the same three people to fill every gap
Check the welfare arrangements: breaks, facilities, and a way to reach someone at three in the morning
strong_answer_signals: Schedules to risk, not evenly
Fatigue managed as a safety issue
Lone working escalation if a check is missed
avoid: Excessive overtime as a normal staffing model
Lone working with no check in procedure
Rotas published days before

questions.text: How do you improve security without a big budget?

key_points: Start with procedure and behaviour, which cost nothing: consistent access control, varied patrols, proper reporting, and door discipline
Fix the basics that are usually broken: lighting, sightlines, overgrown landscaping, unlocked doors, and unreturned passes
Use data: incident locations and times tell you where to put presence, rather than spreading evenly
Deterrence is cheap: visible presence, signage, and a site that looks well maintained. Neglect invites attempts
Train the client staff too, since tailgating and propped doors are usually staff behaviour rather than a system failure
Prioritise honestly and say what the residual risk is after the cheap fixes, so the client can decide
strong_answer_signals: Names procedure and behaviour as the free levers
Uses incident data to place presence
States the residual risk honestly
avoid: Recommending technology as the first answer
Spreading presence evenly regardless of the data
Implying cheap fixes remove the risk entirely

questions.text: Why do you want to work in security?

key_points: Give an honest reason: you are calm under pressure, you like responsibility, you prefer working independently, you want a role where being reliable matters
Connect it to something you have actually done, in work, service, or life
Say what you are good at: observation, staying calm, dealing with people, thoroughness in records
Practical reasons such as shift patterns and stability are respected when paired with genuine interest
strong_answer_signals: An honest reason with evidence behind it
Names calmness and observation rather than authority
Comfortable with practical motivations
avoid: Wanting authority or confrontation
Describing it as a stepping stone to police without saying you value this role
Only saying you need a job

questions.text: How do you stay alert on a long quiet shift?

key_points: Be honest that most shifts are uneventful and that alertness is the actual discipline
Say what you do: vary the patrol timing, active scanning rather than passive watching, move regularly, use the shift for checks that need doing
Manage sleep properly on a night rotation rather than fixing tiredness on shift
Stay off your phone. Say it plainly, since it is the single most common failure
Say what you would do if you genuinely could not stay awake, which is report it rather than hide it
strong_answer_signals: Honest that vigilance is the discipline
Names phone use as the failure
Would report being unfit to continue
avoid: Claiming you never get tired
Phone or entertainment as a way to pass the time
No sleep management on nights

questions.text: What does good security look like to you?

key_points: Prevention rather than response. A quiet site with nothing to report is the product, not a boring shift
Visible, approachable presence that deters without intimidating
Consistency: the same standard at three in the morning as at three in the afternoon
Accurate records, because the report is often the only evidence anything happened at all
Knowing your limits and calling for help early rather than proving something
strong_answer_signals: Values prevention over incident response
Consistency at unsociable hours
Understands records as the evidence of service
avoid: Describing the job as catching people
Equating good security with confrontation
No mention of records or consistency

questions.text: How do you feel about nights, weekends and lone working?

key_points: Be exact and honest. This industry runs on nights, weekends and holidays, and a vague answer becomes a rota problem quickly
Say whether you have worked nights before and how you managed it
State any genuine constraint: transport at night, caring responsibilities, a second job
Say how you feel about being alone on a site, since some people genuinely do not suit it and that is worth knowing now
strong_answer_signals: Exact about availability
Honest about suitability for lone working
States constraints up front
avoid: Saying fully flexible when you are not
Discovering a transport problem after starting
Not having thought about lone working at all

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in a couple of years?

key_points: Honest options: supervisor, control room, CCTV operator, mobile patrol, corporate or specialist sites, close protection, or security management
If you intend to apply to the police or the fire service, say so honestly rather than being caught out
If you want to stay and be excellent at this, say that. Experienced reliable officers are genuinely valued
Name what you would need: a qualification, a licence endorsement, or specific site experience
strong_answer_signals: Honest about other career intentions
Names a step and what it requires
Comfortable saying they want to stay in the role
avoid: Hiding an intention to leave for another service
No thought about progression
Claiming ambitions you do not have

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?

key_points: Ask what tells you what the job actually is:
"What site would I be on, and is it single officer or a team?"
"What are the assignment instructions, and when were they last reviewed?"
"What is the lone working procedure and the check in arrangement?"
"What support is available at night if something happens?"
"What equipment is provided, and what condition is it in?"
The lone working and support question is the most important one you can ask, and the answer tells you how the company treats its officers
strong_answer_signals: Asks about lone working support
Asks when the assignment instructions were last reviewed
Asks about equipment condition
avoid: No questions
Only asking about pay and hours
Asking something already in the job description
